provenance.concepts: share/concepts.json. Framing follows the paradigm-first style of blog.codeminer42.com 'A Noob's Neovim Journey Pt.1' (2024-10-23).
provenance.spine: The `tutor` field on each drill names the vimtutor lesson node it covers. vimtutor ships with vim and neovim ($VIMRUNTIME/tutor/en/); its lesson SEQUENCE is used as the curriculum spine. No vimtutor text is copied.
provenance.drill_shape: concept -> skill -> source -> recipe -> challenge -> mastery counter, the structure used by Vim Hero and vim-adventures lesson trees.
provenance.art: share/art.json, extracted byte-exact from the Stone Story RPG ASCII tutorial plates by share/extract_art.py. Every drill's `source` field names the plate or the numbered rule in the ascii-art-authoring skill that it comes from.

modes.title: Modes: why the editor has more than one rulebook
modes.paradigm:
Every other editor you have used runs in one mode. Every key you press inserts
itself, so every COMMAND has to be smuggled in behind a modifier: Ctrl, Cmd,
Alt, or a menu. That single decision is why those editors need a mouse, and why
your hands leave the home row a hundred times an hour.

Vim makes the opposite trade. It splits editing into modes, and each mode is a
small self-contained module with its own rulebook. In Normal mode the entire
alphabet is free, so commands get to be single letters. In Insert mode the
alphabet means letters again. Nothing has to be smuggled.

  Normal   navigate and operate on text          <Esc>
  Insert   type text like a normal editor        i a o I A O
  Visual   select first, then act                v V <C-v>
  Command  talk to the editor in its own line    :

The cost is real: you have to know which mode you are in, and beginners pay for
that in confusion. The payoff is that commands become composable letters instead
of chords, and composable letters can be multiplied together. That multiplication
is the whole reason the rest of these drills exist.

Practical rule: Normal mode is home. You visit Insert mode, you do not live
there. If you find yourself holding a key down, you are in the wrong mode.

grammar.title: The grammar: vim is a language, not a list of shortcuts
grammar.paradigm:
The single idea that turns vim from a chore into a tool: commands are sentences.

  [count]  [operator]  [motion or text object]
   adverb     verb          noun

  d        w                 delete one word
  2 d      w                 delete two words
  c        i(                change what is inside the parentheses
  y        ap                yank around this paragraph
  >        }                 indent to the end of the paragraph

You do not memorise commands. You memorise a small vocabulary of verbs and a
small vocabulary of nouns, and the editor multiplies them for you. Ten verbs and
thirty nouns is three hundred edits you were never explicitly taught, and you
can guess every one of them.

This is why nobody has to tell you what `yi(` does once you know `ci(`. It is
also why `d` alone does nothing: a verb with no object is not a sentence. The
editor is waiting for the rest of it.

  verbs   c change   d delete   y yank   > indent   gu lowercase   = format
  nouns   w word   $ end of line   } paragraph   f. up to a dot   i( inside parens

When you catch yourself pressing x fifteen times, stop. That is not a sentence,
that is a stutter. Find the noun that names what you actually want to remove.

repeat.title: Repetition: fast editing is repeatable editing, not fast typing
repeat.paradigm:
Watching an expert use vim, the obvious conclusion is that they type quickly.
They do not. What they do is structure each edit so that the editor can perform
it again for them.

Vim gives you three tiers of replay, and they cover almost everything:

  .        repeat the last change, once, wherever the cursor now is
  3a-<Esc> do the insert three times as a single change
  qq ... q record a macro, then @q replays it, 10@q replays it ten times
  :%s///   apply one substitution to every line at once

This has a consequence that is easy to miss: a sloppy edit is a dead end and a
precise edit is an asset. If you fix a line with five improvised keystrokes,
nothing can replay that. If you fix it with `ciw` plus a word, `.` will fix the
next nine occurrences for free. The habit is to make edits small, named, and
repeatable, and then let the editor do the volume.

It is also why `u` (undo) is cheap here. Try a repeatable edit, watch it apply,
undo it if it was wrong. The cost of a wrong guess is one keystroke.

motion-precision.title: Motions: moving the cursor IS editing
motion-precision.paradigm:
In most editors, moving the cursor and changing the text are two different
activities. You arrow over to a spot, then you do a thing. In vim the motion is
an ingredient of the change, so the two collapse into one thought.

  f,     move to the next comma
  df,    delete up to and including the next comma
  ct,    change everything up to but not including the next comma

`df,` is not three keystrokes that happen to be adjacent. It is one intention.
This is why counting keystrokes is the wrong scorecard. The right question is
how many DECISIONS an edit took, and the answer should usually be one.

  f{char}  find the next one on this line      F{char}  find the previous one
  t{char}  stop just before the next one       T{char}  stop just after the previous
  ;        do that find again                  ,        do it backwards
  0 ^ $    start of line, first real char, end of line
  %        bounce between matching brackets    }        next blank line

Precision beats speed. h and l are for adjusting by one cell, not for travelling.
If you are pressing l more than about three times, there was a motion for it.

text-objects.title: Text objects: address the thing, not the coordinates
text-objects.paradigm:
Motions move from where you are to somewhere else, so they depend on where you
happen to be standing. Text objects do not. They name a STRUCTURE, and they work
from anywhere inside it.

  iw  the word            aw  the word plus its trailing space
  i(  inside the parens   a(  the parens as well
  i"  inside the quotes   a"  the quotes as well
  ip  this paragraph      ap  the paragraph plus its blank line
  it  inside the XML tag  at  the tag as well

`ci(` means "change what is inside these parentheses" and the cursor can be on
the opening bracket, the closing bracket, or anywhere in between. You do not have
to navigate to an edge first. You do not have to count characters.

This is the difference between an edit that is robust and an edit that is a
stunt. Position-based edits break the moment the text shifts by one character.
Structure-based edits do not, which is also why they survive being recorded into
a macro and replayed across forty lines.

i = inner (the contents). a = around (the contents plus the delimiters). That is
the whole mnemonic, and it composes with every verb you already know.

lines-and-blocks.title: Lines and blocks: the buffer is two-dimensional
lines-and-blocks.paradigm:
Most text tooling treats a file as one long string with newlines in it. Vim
treats it as a grid, and gives you operators for both axes.

Along the vertical axis, the line operators:

  dd  delete a line     yy  copy a line      p / P  put it back below / above
  3yy 2p                copy three lines, stamp them down twice
  ddp                   swap this line with the one below it
  :t.  :m0              copy this line to here, move this line to there

Along the horizontal axis, blockwise visual mode:

  <C-v>   select a RECTANGLE, not a run of text
  <C-v>jjI|<Esc>   insert a column down three lines at once
  <C-v>jjd         delete a column
  <C-v>jj$A;<Esc>  append to the end of several lines at once

This is the mode that makes monospaced art tractable. An animation file is a
stack of frames; a frame is a rectangle. Copying a frame, erasing one column
across it, or re-sorting frames into playback order are all one-command
operations here, and they are miserable everywhere else.

Gabriel Santos animates Stone Story RPG in a plain text editor for exactly this
reason: the frames are text, so the text editor is the animation tool.

registers-and-ranges.title: Ranges and registers: where the editor becomes a small language
registers-and-ranges.paradigm:
Press `:` and you are no longer pressing keys at an editor, you are issuing
statements to it. Every statement takes a range, and the range is the powerful
half.

  :t.        copy this line to just after this line
  :5,10m0    move lines 5 to 10 to the top of the file
  :%s/o/0/g  substitute across every line in the buffer
  :'<,'>!sort  pipe the visual selection through an external program
  :g/^$/d    run a command on every line matching a pattern

And the yank you did three edits ago is not gone. Vim has a bank of named
clipboards:

  "ayy   yank this line into register a       "ap   put register a back
  "0p    the last yank, even after a delete overwrote the unnamed register
  qa...q record keystrokes into register a, and @a replays them

The macros and the registers are the same storage. A recorded macro is literally
just text in a register, which means you can paste it out, edit it as text, and
yank it back in. That is the point at which the editor stops being a keyboard
game and starts being programmable.

drills.title: spark, one cell
drills.skill: move the cursor, delete a character
drills.source: Stone Story RPG ASCII tutorial page (stonestoryrpg.com/ascii_tutorial.html) plate 01, particle layer frame 4 The particle layer is a one-cell animation.
keys: h j k l   left down up right, without leaving the home row
dd  delete a line     x  delete a character     u  undo
drills.buys: The home-row four. Every motion you learn later replaces these.

drills.title: trim the alphabet
recipe: delete the word under the cursor, and the space after it
drills.source: Stone Story RPG ASCII tutorial page (stonestoryrpg.com/ascii_tutorial.html) plate 03 section 5, the four extended glyphs
keys: dw   delete a word        de   delete to the end of the word
d$   delete to end of line   dd   delete the line
drills.buys: The first verb+noun sentence: delete, a word.

drills.title: cut the label
recipe: jump to the end of the line
back to the space before the label
delete from here to the end of the line
drills.source: Stone Story RPG ASCII tutorial page (stonestoryrpg.com/ascii_tutorial.html) plate 03, Line style The plate labels the style beside the art.
keys: D = d$   delete to end of line      C = c$   change to end of line
F<char>  find backwards on this line
drills.buys: Stripping a label off a line without counting characters.

drills.title: two runs on
drills.skill: use a count with a motion
recipe: delete two WORDS. Capital W, and here is why:
w stops at every punctuation mark, and line art is all punctuation.
W is whitespace-delimited, so one run is one W.
drills.source: Stone Story RPG ASCII tutorial page (stonestoryrpg.com/ascii_tutorial.html) plate 04 section 6, the classic _.-´ stair-step Three copies of the stair-step run.
keys: w  next word, stopping at punctuation     W  next whitespace-delimited WORD
b B  backwards        e E  end of word
d2W  delete two runs                      3dd  delete three lines
For prose, w. For art, W: `_.-´` is four words to w and one WORD to W.
drills.buys: The w/W distinction, on material where it actually bites.

drills.title: drop a frame
recipe: move down to the third frame's apex
drills.source: Stone Story RPG ASCII tutorial page (stonestoryrpg.com/ascii_tutorial.html) plate 06, apex rows of pyramid frames 1 to 5
keys: dd   delete a line      3dd  delete three lines      D  delete to end of line
drills.buys: Frames are lines. Dropping one is one command.

drills.title: delete, then think again
recipe: undo it. The line comes back.
redo it. Ctrl and r. The line goes away again.
drills.source: Stone Story RPG ASCII tutorial page (stonestoryrpg.com/ascii_tutorial.html) plate 06, apex rows of pyramid frames 1 to 5
keys: u      undo the last change        <C-r>  redo
U      undo every change on this line
Undo is cheap. That is what makes guessing a command a reasonable move.
drills.buys: Nothing you try in normal mode costs more than one keystroke to take back.

drills.title: stamp a spark
recipe: put the yanked line below it
drills.source: Stone Story RPG ASCII tutorial page (stonestoryrpg.com/ascii_tutorial.html) plate 01, particle layer frame 1
keys: yy  yank a line    p  put below    P  put above    3p  put three copies
drills.buys: Copy and paste, without a clipboard or a mouse.

drills.title: raise the joint
drills.source: skill §4.6 rule 5: a joint glyph sits differently in its cell. `.` sits too low, `'` sits too high, `:` sits in the middle.
keys: r<char>  replace one character, staying in normal mode
3rx      replace the next three          R  overwrite until <Esc>
drills.buys: One glyph, one key, no mode change.

drills.title: stair-step run
recipe: change the word under the cursor
type the run, then the same run mirrored
drills.source: skill §4.7 drills 1-2: type the stair-step run, then type it mirrored. Plated as `_.-´` in the Lines & Materials section.
keys: cw   change to end of word      ciw  change the word from anywhere in it
The plate writes the rise as _ . - ´ . That last glyph is an acute accent,
not an apostrophe. The `symbol table` drill shows how to get it.
drills.buys: The verb+noun sentence, on the run you will type more than any other.

drills.title: shallowest gradient
recipe: change from the cursor to the end of the line
save and quit, no colon needed
drills.source: skill §4.4: `,` and `.` runs give the shallowest gradient available.
keys: C = c$  change to end of line      A  append at end of line
0  start of line   ^  first non-blank   $  end of line
ZZ save and quit                   ZQ quit without saving
drills.buys: The shorthand verbs: each is a contraction of a whole sentence.

drills.title: find the anchor
recipe: delete the line it landed on
drills.source: Stone Story RPG ASCII tutorial page (stonestoryrpg.com/ascii_tutorial.html) plate 05 section 10, the dithered sphere, lower band
keys: /text  search forward    ?text  search backward
n      next match        N      previous match
<C-o>  jump back to where you were      <C-i>  jump forward again
drills.buys: Finding a cell by what is in it, not by counting to it.

drills.title: check the pair
recipe: change INSIDE the parentheses. The brackets survive.
three spaces, an apostrophe, three spaces
bounce between the brackets to check the pair
drills.source: Stone Story RPG ASCII tutorial page (stonestoryrpg.com/ascii_tutorial.html) plate 03, Line style This is the lamp's body row.
keys: %    jump between matching ( ) [ ] { }
ci(  change inside parens     ca(  change the parens as well
The cursor may sit anywhere inside the object.
drills.buys: i = inner, a = around. One mnemonic, a hundred commands.

drills.title: swap one glyph
recipe: substitute, but the dot means `any character` in a pattern
drills.source: skill §4.6 rule 5: `:` sits at mid-height in the cell, `.` sits too low.
keys: :s/old/new/     first match on this line
:s/old/new/g    every match on this line
:%s/old/new/g   every match in the file
In a pattern, . means any character. Escape it as \. to mean a literal dot.
drills.buys: The first taste of the colon line, and of patterns.

drills.title: lighten every band
recipe: on every line, replace each :: with .:
drills.source: skill §8 rule 2: lighten a shading band by erasing members of it, not by swapping to a lighter glyph.
keys: :%s/a/b/g    every match in the file
:%s/a/b/gc   ask for confirmation at each one
:5,9s/a/b/g  only on lines 5 to 9
drills.buys: One command instead of forty edits.

drills.title: pad the frame
recipe: open a blank line ABOVE the cursor
drills.source: Stone Story RPG ASCII tutorial page (stonestoryrpg.com/ascii_tutorial.html) plate 01, particle layer frame 1 skill §9 step h: pad every frame to the height of the tallest one before rendering.
keys: o  open a line below and start typing      O  open one above
Frames in a set must be the same height, so padding is routine.
drills.buys: Padding frames to a common height, one keystroke per row.

drills.title: ground the run
recipe: append at the end of the line
then put the acute accent there
drills.source: skill §4.4: the classic stair-step is `_ . - ´`. If your keyboard cannot type ´ directly, do the `symbol table` drill instead.
keys: a  append after the cursor      A  append at end of line
i  insert before the cursor     I  insert before the first non-blank
drills.buys: Four ways into insert mode, each saving a motion.

drills.title: hold a spark
recipe: put a copy of it below
drills.source: Stone Story RPG ASCII tutorial page (stonestoryrpg.com/ascii_tutorial.html) plate 01, particle layer frame 2 skill §10: a hold is a repeated frame.
keys: yy p   the cheapest duplicate there is
3yy    yank three lines      "ayy   yank into register a
drills.buys: A hold in animation is a repeated frame, and two keystrokes here.

drills.title: close the seam
recipe: join the next line onto this one, with a space between
drills.source: skill §4.7 drill 2: type the run, then type it mirrored.
keys: J   join the line below, inserting a space
gJ  join without inserting anything
3J  join three lines
drills.buys: Two rows become one row without retyping either.

drills.title: swap the eye
drills.source: skill §4.3 rule 3: place one alphanumeric only where you want the reader to look, such as an eye. Both `o` and `O` are on the twelve-glyph whitelist.
keys: ~    toggle the case of one character      3~   toggle three
g~w  toggle the case of a word             gUU  upper-case the line
drills.buys: The smallest possible edit, and a real one: o and O read as different eyes.

drills.title: around versus inside
recipe: land on the apostrophe inside the brackets
change AROUND the parens: the brackets go too
drills.source: Stone Story RPG ASCII tutorial page (stonestoryrpg.com/ascii_tutorial.html) plate 03, Line style
keys: ci(  change inside the parens       ca(  change the parens as well
di"  delete inside quotes           dap  delete a paragraph and its blank line
i = inner, a = around.
drills.buys: The difference between the contents and the container.

drills.title: drop a layer
recipe: delete that paragraph AND its blank separator
drills.source: Stone Story RPG ASCII tutorial page (stonestoryrpg.com/ascii_tutorial.html) plate 01, particle layer frame 1 skill §3 rule 5: layers are stored as blank-line-separated blocks in one file, back layer first.
keys: dap  delete a paragraph and its blank line    dip  just the paragraph
yap  yank one                                 }    jump to the next blank line
A blank-line-separated block IS a layer. That is why ap matters here.
drills.buys: A frame or a layer is a paragraph. Address it as one.

drills.title: two glyphs at once
recipe: yank this line into register a
put register a OVER the selection
drills.source: skill §1.7: keep a symbol-table file of glyphs open beside the drawing. Named registers are that table, inside the editor.
keys: "ayy  yank a line into register a      "ap  put it back
"Ayy  APPEND to register a             :reg  list every register
Twenty-six registers means twenty-six glyphs held at once.
drills.buys: A bank of clipboards, which is what glyph work actually needs.

drills.title: the yank survives
recipe: delete it. That overwrites the unnamed register, but NOT register 0.
put register 0: the last YANK, not the last delete
drills.source: skill §1.7, the symbol-table workflow: a delete must not cost you the glyph you just copied.
keys: "0p   the last yank, even after a delete overwrote the unnamed register
"1p   the last delete    "2p  the one before that
This is the fix for `I yanked, then deleted, and my yank was gone`.
drills.buys: Why your paste stopped working, and the register that fixes it.

drills.title: back to the anchor
recipe: drop mark a on this line
jump straight back to mark a
drills.source: Stone Story RPG ASCII tutorial page (stonestoryrpg.com/ascii_tutorial.html) plate 06, apex rows of pyramid frames 1 to 5
keys: ma   set mark a here      'a   jump to the line of mark a
`a   jump to the exact cell of mark a      :marks  list them
d'a  delete from here to mark a
drills.buys: A bookmark, so a long file stops costing you your place.

drills.title: select and cut
recipe: extend the selection down two lines
drills.source: Stone Story RPG ASCII tutorial page (stonestoryrpg.com/ascii_tutorial.html) plate 06, apex rows of pyramid frames 1 to 5
keys: v   character-wise    V   line-wise    <C-v>  block-wise
gv  reselect whatever you had selected last
o   in visual mode, jump to the other end of the selection
drills.buys: Select first, then act, for when you cannot name the motion.

drills.title: column of bars
recipe: capital I: insert at the LEFT edge of the block
leave insert mode. The bar lands on all three lines.
drills.source: skill §4.4: the rotation triple is `\` then `\|` then `/`; the vertical bar is the in-between frame.
keys: <C-v>jjI text <Esc>   insert down a column
<C-v>jj$A text <Esc>  append to the end of several lines
<C-v>jjd              delete a column
Nothing appears to happen until you press <Esc>.
drills.buys: Editing a rectangle. Frame work is rectangle work.

drills.title: rotation in-between
recipe: extend to the end of every line
capital A: append after the block
drills.source: skill §4.4: `\` then `\|` then `/` is the rotation triple. The bar is the tween.
keys: <C-v>jj$A  appends to lines of different lengths, correctly
<C-v>jjI   inserts at a fixed column instead
drills.buys: The in-between frame of a rotation, in one command.

drills.title: narrow the base
recipe: move onto the first bar of the base
extend down two lines and right two columns
delete the rectangle. The base loses one unit.
drills.source: Stone Story RPG ASCII tutorial page (stonestoryrpg.com/ascii_tutorial.html) plate 06 section 13, subtractive-animation pyramid, frame 1 of 7 skill §10: copy the frame, delete one unit, repeat.
keys: <C-v>jjd   delete a rectangle      <C-v>jjr.  fill it with one glyph
Subtractive animation: draw the finished object, erase one unit per frame,
then re-sort the frames into playback order.
drills.buys: Erasing a unit per frame is how accretive animation is really authored.

drills.title: fill a rectangle
recipe: extend down two lines and right one column
replace every cell in the rectangle
drills.source: skill §8: a shading band is built by alternating two glyphs across a region.
keys: <C-v>...r<char>  fill a rectangle with one glyph
<C-v>...~        toggle case across a rectangle
<C-v>...d        cut it out
drills.buys: Repainting a region without touching the cells around it.

drills.title: frame caps
recipe: cap the start of the line
cap the end of the line
step down. Recording the move is what makes it replayable.
drills.source: skill §4.6 rule 5: `'` sits high in its cell, so it caps a frame cleanly.
keys: qa ... q  record into register a     @a   replay      10@a  replay ten times
@@        replay the last macro again
Always record the move to the next item as part of the macro.
"ap pastes a macro out as text, so you can edit it and yank it back.
drills.buys: Teaching the editor a new verb, in about four seconds.

drills.title: the symbol table
drills.skill: yank a glyph, put it over another
recipe: jump to the first extended glyph
drop to the slope line, last character: the wrong glyph
select that character and put the yanked one over it
drills.source: skill §1.7: keep the glyph alphabet open beside the drawing. skill §4.2: ´ is the mirror of the backtick. It is not the apostrophe, and it is not on your keyboard.
keys: yl   yank one character         3yl  yank three
vp   select, then put OVER the selection
This is how an artist types a glyph the keyboard does not have: keep a
strip of them in the file and copy from it. Never retype by hand.
drills.buys: The four extended glyphs, without fighting your keyboard layout.

drills.title: walk an edit down
recipe: step down. The dot repeats r: at the SAME column.
drills.source: skill §4.6 rule 5: `.` sits too low, `'` too high, `:` in the middle.
keys: j keeps your column, so j. walks one edit down a stack of frames
3.  repeat the change three times
For a taller stack, record it: qq r: j q  then 20@q
drills.buys: Vertical repetition without a macro.

drills.title: hop the band
recipe: delete from here to the end of the line
drills.source: skill §8: a shading band alternates two glyphs, which makes it a row of landmarks.
keys: f:  find next :     F:  find previous :     ;  repeat     ,  reverse
t:  stop just BEFORE the next :            df:  delete up to and including it
drills.buys: Travelling by landmark instead of counting cells.

drills.title: duplicate a base row
recipe: copy THIS line to just after itself. Colon, t, dot.
drills.source: Stone Story RPG ASCII tutorial page (stonestoryrpg.com/ascii_tutorial.html) plate 06 section 13, subtractive-animation pyramid, frame 1 of 7 The base rows of the pyramid.
keys: :t.   copy this line below itself     :t0  copy it to the top
:m0   move this line to the top       :m$  move it to the bottom
yyp does the same as :t. Ranges scale to a hundred lines; yyp does not.
drills.buys: The colon line takes a range, and the range is the half that scales.

drills.title: hold a walk frame
recipe: yank six lines: the whole frame
drills.source: Stone Story RPG ASCII tutorial page (stonestoryrpg.com/ascii_tutorial.html) plate 02, Poison Adept walk cycle, frame 1 of 10 skill §10: add holds by repeating frames.
keys: 6yy 2p  copy a 6-line frame and stamp it down twice
yap p   yank a blank-line-separated frame and put it
P       put ABOVE the cursor instead of below
drills.buys: A real frame, copied the way a real frame file gets built.

drills.title: tween by copy and edit
drills.skill: copy a frame, change one row
recipe: copy it below. That copy is now frame 2.
fourth row of the copy, last cell
step back: the accent becomes a comma
drills.source: Stone Story RPG ASCII tutorial page (stonestoryrpg.com/ascii_tutorial.html) plate 02, Poison Adept walk cycle, frame 1 of 10 Frames 1 and 2 differ in exactly one row. skill §10: preserve the glyph pattern between frames wherever the part has not changed.
keys: Copy the previous frame, then change ONLY the cells that move. Everything
you do not touch stays registered, which is what stops an animation boiling.
yyp then edit     the cheapest tween there is
<C-v> then r      change a rectangle between frames
drills.buys: Temporal coherence: every frame is an edit of the frame before it.

drills.title: break the seam
recipe: find the slash that joins the two forms
replace it with an acute accent, which does not touch the other form
(if ´ is hard to type, do the `symbol table` drill first)
drills.source: Stone Story RPG ASCII tutorial page (stonestoryrpg.com/ascii_tutorial.html) plate 05 section 9, two forms sharing a seam glyph skill §3: a glyph shared between two objects creates a false connection. Replace it with a partial-coverage glyph placed away from the seam.
keys: The plate shows this edit as a before/after pair, with an arrow between them.
It is two character replacements, and it is the whole depth technique:
a shared glyph reads as a join           break it
a deleted cell at a seam reads as shadow leave it empty
drills.buys: Depth, from one character. This is the highest-value edit in the whole method.

drills.title: playback order
recipe: delete this line and put it back after the next. They swap.
drills.source: Stone Story RPG ASCII tutorial page (stonestoryrpg.com/ascii_tutorial.html) plate 06, apex rows of pyramid frames 1 to 5 skill §10: authoring order and playback order are independent; re-sort the frames afterwards.
keys: ddp    swap with the line below      ddkP  swap with the line above
:m+1   move this line down one       :m-2  move it up one
:5,9m0 move a range to the top
drills.buys: Re-sorting frames is one idiom, not a rewrite.

drills.title: one edit, every row
drills.skill: run a normal command over a range
recipe: select from here to the last line
press colon. Vim fills in the range '<,'> for you.
run `A'` in normal mode on every selected line
drills.source: skill §4.4: `'` plus `´` reads as a very slight inclination; capping a run is a per-row edit you want to apply to the whole set at once.
keys: :'<,'>normal A;   append ; to every selected line
:%normal I// commentiment every line in the file
:g/pattern/cmd    run cmd on every MATCHING line (whole buffer -- careful)
Selecting first and then pressing : is how you scope a range safely.
drills.buys: Any normal-mode command, applied to a whole range at once.

drills.title: hand-mirrored run
recipe: replace the underscore with a dash
step right, replace with a period
step right, replace with an underscore
drills.source: skill §4.7 drills 6-7: mirror art by retyping the row backwards with each glyph swapped for its mirror. Never use a software flip.
keys: The mirror table:  _ <-> _    . <-> .    - <-> -
r<char>  replace one character      3rx  replace three
drills.buys: Mirroring by hand, which is the only way that preserves the style.

drills.title: pad to height
recipe: the dot repeats the whole open-line change
drills.source: Stone Story RPG ASCII tutorial page (stonestoryrpg.com/ascii_tutorial.html) plate 01, particle layer frame 1 skill §9 step h: count the rows in the tallest frame and pad every other frame to that height before rendering.
keys: O<Esc> then .   pad a frame one row at a time
3O<Esc>         or do it in one count
A frame set of mixed heights renders as a jitter.
drills.buys: The least glamorous step in animation, reduced to two keystrokes.

drills.title: cap every frame
drills.skill: replay a macro over a frame set
recipe: select it and the one after it
step to the next frame row
replay it on the remaining four
drills.source: skill §8: a shading band is a region of alternating glyphs, applied per frame.
keys: qq ... q then 4@q   the same edit across a whole frame set
A macro beats the dot when the edit is more than one operator.
If a macro goes wrong, u undoes the whole replay one step at a time.
drills.buys: One recorded edit, applied to every frame in the set.
